claim: The house mouse features a rare combination of sophisticated genetic tools and natural hybrid zones between subspecies.
source: The house mouse features a rare combination of sophisticated genetic tools and natural hybrid zones between subspecies.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract about the characteristics of the house mouse as a model system.

claim: Male hybrids often show reduced fertility, a common reproductive barrier between incipient species.
source: Male hybrids often show reduced fertility, a common reproductive barrier between incipient species.
evidence: This statement is supported by general knowledge about reproductive barriers and is referenced in the context of the study.

claim: Laboratory crosses have identified sterility loci, but each encompasses hundreds of genes.
source: Laboratory crosses have identified sterility loci, but each encompasses hundreds of genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to previous laboratory studies mentioned throughout the manuscript.

claim: Many generations of admixture enables high-resolution mapping of loci contributing to sterility-related phenotypes.
source: Many generations of admixture enables high-resolution mapping of loci contributing to these sterility-related phenotypes.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the advantage of using hybrid zone populations, supported by the study design and results.

claim: Multiple, non-independent genetic incompatibilities contribute to barriers to gene flow in the hybrid zone.
source: We identify complex interactions among sterility loci, suggesting multiple, non-independent genetic incompatibilities contribute to barriers to gene flow in the hybrid zone.
evidence: This claim is supported by the interaction analysis results presented in the study.

claim: New species arise when reproductive barriers form, preventing gene flow between populations.
source: New species arise when reproductive barriers form, preventing gene flow between populations (Coyne and Orr, 2004).
evidence: This is a fundamental principle of speciation supported by citation.

claim: Islands of divergence have been reported in species pairs from taxonomically diverse groups.
source: For example, 'islands of divergence' have been reported in species pairs from taxonomically diverse groups (Turner et al., 2005; Nadeau et al., 2011; Nosil et al., 2012; Ellegren et al., 2013; Hemmer-Hansen et al., 2013; Renaut et al., 2013; Carneiro et al., 2014; Poelstra et al., 2014; Schumer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Islands of divergence may not always represent targets of selection that contributed to speciation.
source: However, other forces can create similar genomic patterns, thus islands may not always represent targets of selection that contributed to speciation (Noor and Bennett, 2009; Turner and Hahn, 2010; Renaut et al., 2013; Cruickshank and Hahn, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies discussing alternative explanations for genomic patterns.

claim: The Dobzhansky-Muller model predicts that hybrid incompatibilities between incipient species accumulate faster than linearly with time.
source: The Dobzhansky-Muller model predicts that hybrid incompatibilities between incipient species accumulate faster than linearly with time (Orr, 1995), thus investigating taxa in the early stages of speciation facilitates identification of incompatibilities that initially caused reproductive isolation vs incompatibilities that arose after isolation was complete.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Orr's theoretical work.

claim: Three house mouse subspecies—M. m. musculus, M. m. domesticus, and M. m. castaneus–diverged ∼500,000 years ago from a common ancestor.
source: Three house mouse subspecies—M. m. musculus, M. m. domesticus, and M. m. castaneus–diverged ∼500,000 years ago from a common ancestor (Reviewed in Boursot et al. (1993); Salcedo et al. (2007); Geraldes et al. (2008)).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple review articles and studies.

claim: M. m. musculus and M. m. domesticus colonized Europe through different geographic routes and meet in a narrow secondary contact zone running through central Europe from Bulgaria to Denmark.
source: M. m. musculus and M. m. domesticus (hereafter, musculus and domesticus) colonized Europe through different geographic routes and meet in a narrow secondary contact zone running through central Europe from Bulgaria to Denmark (Sage et al., 1986; Boursot et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies documenting the geographic distribution and colonization history.

claim: Reduced male fertility is common in wild-caught hybrids.
source: Reduced male fertility is common in wild-caught hybrids (Albrechtová et al., 2012; Turner et al., 2012) and in musculus–domesticus hybrids generated in the laboratory (Britton-Davidian et al., 2005; Reviewed in Good et al. (2008a)), implying that hybrid sterility is an important barrier to gene flow in house mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies of wild-caught and laboratory hybrids.

claim: Prdm9 was recently identified as a gene causing F1 hybrid sterility and is the first mammalian hybrid incompatibility gene identified.
source: Prdm9, a histone methyltransferase, was recently identified as a gene causing F1 hybrid sterility and is the first mammalian hybrid incompatibility gene identified (Mihola et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the study that identified Prdm9.

claim: Hybrid sterility alleles are polymorphic within subspecies.
source: Comparisons between different F1 crosses show that hybrid sterility alleles are polymorphic within subspecies (Britton-Davidian et al., 2005; Good et al., 2008a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies comparing different crosses.

claim: Complete sterility appears to be rare or absent in the hybrid zone.
source: Furthermore, reduced fertility phenotypes observed in nature vary in severity; complete sterility, as documented in some F1 crosses, appears to be rare or absent in the hybrid zone (Albrechtová et al., 2012; Turner et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies of fertility in the hybrid zone.

claim: The mapping population includes 185 first generation lab-bred male offspring of mice captured in the hybrid zone.
source: We performed a genome-wide association study (GWAS) to map testis weight and testis gene expression in 185 first generation lab-bred offspring of wild-caught hybrid mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study design and sample size.

claim: Testis expression PC1 explains 14.6% of the variance.
source: Testis expression PC1 (explaining 14.6% of the variance) is significantly correlated with relative testis weight (cor = 0.67, P = 2 × 10−16), indicating that there is a strong association between those two sterility phenotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the principal component analysis results.

claim: Testis expression PC1 is significantly correlated with relative testis weight (cor = 0.67, P = 2 × 10−16).
source: Testis expression PC1 (explaining 14.6% of the variance) is significantly correlated with relative testis weight (cor = 0.67, P = 2 × 10−16), indicating that there is a strong association between those two sterility phenotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the phenotypic data.

claim: Principal component 2 (PC2, 8.1% variance) is strongly correlated with hybrid index (% musculus autosomal SNPs: cor = 0.75, P = 2 × 10−16).
source: Principal component 2 (PC2, 8.1% variance) is strongly correlated with hybrid index (% musculus autosomal SNPs: cor = 0.75, P = 2 × 10−16), thus the effect of hybrid defects does not obscure subspecies differences in expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing correlation between PC2 and ancestry.

claim: 10.2% of individuals had relative testis weight below the minimum observed in pure subspecies males.
source: In the mapping population, 19/185 (10.2%) individuals had relative testis weight below the minimum observed in pure subspecies males and 21/179 (11.7%) individuals had expression PC1 scores below (PC1 = −46.97) the pure subspecies range.
evidence: This claim is supported by direct measurement and comparison of phenotypes.

claim: 11.7% of individuals had expression PC1 scores below the pure subspecies range.
source: In the mapping population, 19/185 (10.2%) individuals had relative testis weight below the minimum observed in pure subspecies males and 21/179 (11.7%) individuals had expression PC1 scores below (PC1 = −46.97) the pure subspecies range.
evidence: This claim is supported by direct measurement and comparison of phenotypes.

claim: Four SNPs significantly associated with relative testis weight were identified in three regions on the X chromosome using stringent thresholds determined by permutation.
source: We identified four SNPs significantly associated with relative testis weight in three regions on the X chromosome using stringent thresholds determined by permutation (Table 1; Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the GWAS results presented in Table 1 and Figure 1A.

claim: An additional 51 SNPs were significant using a more permissive significance threshold (false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.1).
source: An additional 51 SNPs were significant using a more permissive significance threshold (false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the GWAS results using FDR threshold.

claim: Significant SNPs were clustered in 12 genomic regions (of size 1 bp to 13.3 Mb).
source: Significant SNPs were clustered in 12 genomic regions (of size 1 bp to 13.3 Mb; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the clustering analysis of significant SNPs reported in Table 1.

claim: Significant regions were located on the X chromosome and 9 autosomes, suggesting a minimum of 10 loci contribute to variation in testis weight.
source: Significant regions were located on the X chromosome and 9 autosomes, suggesting a minimum of 10 loci contribute to variation in testis weight.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the distribution of significant regions across chromosomes.

claim: 104 SNPs on the X and chromosome 1 were significantly associated with expression PC1 using stringent permutation-based thresholds.
source: We identified 104 SNPs on the X and chromosome 1 significantly associated with expression PC1 using stringent permutation-based thresholds (Table 2; Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the GWAS results presented in Table 2 and Figure 1B.

claim: An additional 349 SNPs were significant with the more permissive threshold of FDR < 0.1 for expression PC1.
source: An additional 349 SNPs were significant with the more permissive threshold of FDR < 0.1.
evidence: This claim is supported by the GWAS results using FDR threshold for expression PC1.

claim: Significant SNPs for expression PC1 clustered in 50 genomic regions located on 18 autosomes and the X.
source: Significant SNPs clustered in 50 genomic regions located on 18 autosomes and the X.
evidence: This claim is supported by the clustering analysis of significant SNPs for expression PC1.

claim: There was substantial overlap between mapping results for testis weight and expression PC1; 48/55 SNPs significant for relative testis weight (9 regions) were also significant for expression PC1.
source: There was substantial overlap between mapping results for testis weight and expression PC1; 48/55 SNPs significant for relative testis weight (9 regions) were also significant for expression PC1.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of GWAS results for the two phenotypes.

claim: A permutation test provides strong evidence that the overlap between testis weight and expression PC1 mapping results is non-random (p < 0.0001, 10,000 permutations).
source: A permutation test, performed by randomly shuffling the positions of GWAS regions in the genome, provides strong evidence that this overlap is non-random (p < 0.0001, 10,000 permutations).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical testing using permutations.

claim: Most SNPs significant for testis weight and/or expression PC1 were significantly enriched for trans associations with individual transcripts.
source: Most SNPs significant for testis weight and/or expression PC1 were significantly enriched for trans associations with individual transcripts (relative testis weight: 49/55 SNPs, 8/12 regions; PC1: 440/453 SNPs, 50/50 regions).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of trans eQTL associations.

claim: 142 significant pairwise interactions for relative testis weight were identified, representing 22 pairs of GWAS regions.
source: We identified 142 significant pairwise interactions for relative testis weight, representing 22 pairs of GWAS regions (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the epistasis analysis results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The interaction results provide evidence for a minimum of 13 autosomal–autosomal and five X–autosomal interactions affecting testis weight.
source: These results provide evidence for a minimum of 13 autosomal–autosomal and five X–autosomal interactions affecting testis weight.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the interaction analysis results.

claim: 44,145 significant interactions between SNPs for expression PC1 were identified.
source: We identified 44,145 significant interactions between SNPs for expression PC1.
evidence: This claim is supported by the epistasis analysis results for expression PC1.

claim: The 913 GWAS region pairs provide evidence that at least 144 autosomal–autosomal interactions and 18 X–autosomal interactions contribute to expression PC1.
source: The 913 GWAS region pairs provide evidence that at least 144 autosomal–autosomal interactions and 18 X–autosomal interactions contribute to expression PC1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the interaction analysis results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Interactions had greater effects, on average, than single loci for both phenotypes.
source: As expected, interactions had greater effects, on average, than single loci for both phenotypes (relative testis weight: single locus mean = −1.81 mg/g, interaction mean = −4.07 mg/g; expression PC1: single locus mean = −81.51, interaction mean = −130.77).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of effect sizes for single loci vs interactions.

claim: The lowest genotypic means for most interactions fell below the range observed in pure subspecies.
source: The lowest genotypic means for most interactions fell below the range observed in pure subspecies (relative testis weight: 19/22 (86.3%) region pairs; expression PC1: 877/913 (96%) region pairs; Figure 3A,B), consistent with the hypothesis that interactions represent Dobzhansky–Muller incompatibilities.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of interaction effects to pure subspecies phenotypes, shown in Figure 3.

claim: The power to detect causative loci depended on the location (autosomal vs X-linked), dominance, and frequency of both 'causative' alleles.
source: As expected, the power to detect one or both causative loci depended on the location (autosomal vs X-linked), dominance, and frequency of both 'causative' alleles (Figure 4, Table 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results presented in Figure 4 and Table 3.

claim: The majority of significant SNPs (62.7%) are within 10 Mb of the causal SNP.
source: The distribution of distances to the causal SNP for all significant SNPs located on the same chromosome (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) shows that the majority of significant SNPs (62.7%) are within 10 Mb of the causal SNP, however, a small proportion of significant SNPs are >50 Mb from the causal SNP.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of simulation results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: 83.4% of loci with significant SNPs 1–10 Mb distant also have significant SNPs within 1 Mb.
source: In most cases, causal SNPs detected at long distances also had significant SNPs nearby, for example 83.4% of loci with significant SNPs 1–10 Mb distant also have significant SNPs within 1 Mb.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of simulation results.

claim: Most sterility loci interact with more than one partner locus.
source: Most sterility loci interact with more than one partner locus.
evidence: This claim is supported by the interaction analysis results showing multiple interactions per locus.

claim: All loci except one showed evidence for interaction with at least one partner locus.
source: All loci except one showed evidence for interaction with at least one partner locus and most interact with more than one partner.
evidence: This claim is supported by the interaction analysis results.

claim: A majority of GWAS regions contain 10 or fewer genes.
source: Using natural hybrids provided high mapping resolution that will facilitate future studies to identify causative genes; for example, a majority of GWAS regions contain 10 or fewer genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene annotation analysis of GWAS regions.

claim: Significant regions identified in the hybrid zone (median = 2.1 Mb) are much smaller than sterility QTL identified in F2s (35.1 Mb).
source: For example, significant regions identified here (median = 2.1 Mb, regions with defined intervals) are much smaller than sterility QTL identified in F2s (35.1 Mb; White et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of region sizes between this study and previous F2 mapping studies.

claim: Several of the loci identified in natural hybrids are novel.
source: Several of the loci identified in this study of hybrid zone mice are novel, providing additional evidence that sterility alleles are polymorphic within subspecies.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with previously identified loci and inference about polymorphism.

claim: A majority of loci identified in natural hybrids are concordant with previously identified sterility QTL.
source: However, a majority of loci we identified in natural hybrids are concordant with previously identified sterility QTL (Tables 1–2, Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with previous studies as shown in Tables 1-2 and Figure 2.

claim: There was no statistical support that genome-wide patterns of overlap with previous studies for testis weight or expression PC1 were non-random.
source: This similarity suggests that there are common genetic factors underlying hybrid sterility in house mice, although there was no statistical support that genome-wide patterns of overlap with previous studies for testis weight or expression PC1 were non-random (p > 0.05, 10,000 permutations).
evidence: This claim is supported by permutation testing of overlap patterns.

claim: None of the GWAS regions identified overlap Prdm9 (chromosome 17, 15.7 Mb).
source: None of the GWAS regions identified here overlap Prdm9 (chromosome 17, 15.7 Mb).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of GWAS region positions with the known location of Prdm9.

claim: One expression PC1 region (PC42) is ∼4 Mb proximal to Prdm9.
source: However, one expression PC1 region (PC42) is ∼4 Mb proximal to Prdm9.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of genomic positions.

claim: Three GWAS regions associated with testis weight are located on the X chromosome.
source: Three GWAS regions associated with testis weight and five expression PC1 regions are located on the X chromosome.
evidence: This claim is supported by the GWAS results showing X-linked associations.

claim: Five expression PC1 regions are located on the X chromosome.
source: Three GWAS regions associated with testis weight and five expression PC1 regions are located on the X chromosome.
evidence: This claim is supported by the GWAS results showing X-linked associations.

claim: The X-chromosomal regions surpass the stringent permutation-based significance thresholds.
source: The X-chromosomal regions surpass the stringent permutation-based significance thresholds and thus have strong statistical support.
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical significance testing results.

claim: Domesticus alleles were associated with the sterile pattern for most loci identified on the X in hybrid zone mice.
source: By contrast, domesticus alleles were associated with the sterile pattern for most loci we identified on the X in hybrid zone mice (Tables 1–2).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of allele effects shown in Tables 1-2.

claim: F1 hybrids are essentially absent in nature because the hybrid zone is ≥30 km wide.
source: F1 hybrids are essentially absent in nature (Teeter et al., 2008; Turner et al., 2012) because the hybrid zone is ≥30 km wide (Boursot et al., 1993), thus pure subspecies individuals rarely encounter each other.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies of hybrid zone structure and F1 frequency.

claim: Recessive autosomal loci acting in F2 and advanced generation hybrids contribute to the maintenance of reproductive isolation in the hybrid zone.
source: Consequently, recessive autosomal loci acting in F2 and advanced generation hybrids contribute to the maintenance of reproductive isolation in the hybrid zone and may have played important roles in its establishment.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the genetic architecture results and hybrid zone structure.

claim: The mapping population includes 185 mice generated from 63 mating pairs involving 37 unrelated females and 35 unrelated males.
source: We included 185 mice generated from 63 mating pairs involving 37 unrelated females and 35 unrelated males.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study design.

claim: Males were housed individually after weaning (28 days) to prevent effects of dominance interactions on fertility.
source: Males were housed individually after weaning (28 days) to prevent effects of dominance interactions on fertility.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental protocol.

claim: Combined testis weight and body weight were measured immediately after mice were sacrificed at 9–12 weeks.
source: We measured combined testis weight and body weight immediately after mice were sacrificed at 9–12 weeks.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the phenotyping protocol.

claim: There is a significant association between testis weight and body weight (Pearson's correlation = 0.29, p = 4.9 × 10−5).
source: We calculated relative testis weight (testis weight/body weight) to account for a significant association between testis weight and body weight (Pearson's correlation = 0.29, p = 4.9 × 10−5).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the phenotypic data.

claim: Gene expression was measured in testes of 179 out of the 185 males from the mapping population.
source: We measured gene expression in testes of 179 out of the 185 males from the mapping population.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the sample size for expression analysis.

claim: The Whole Mouse Genome Microarray contains 43,379 probes surveying 22,210 transcripts from 21,326 genes.
source: This array contains 43,379 probes surveying 22,210 transcripts from 21,326 genes.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the microarray platform specifications.

claim: A total of 36,323 probes (covering 19,742 Entrez Genes) were retained after filtering.
source: A total of 36,323 probes (covering 19,742 Entrez Genes) were retained.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data processing results.

claim: Males from the mapping population were genotyped using Mouse Diversity Genotyping Arrays.
source: Males from the mapping population were genotyped using Mouse Diversity Genotyping Arrays (Affymetrix, Santa Clara, CA) by Atlas Biolabs (Berlin, Germany).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the genotyping method.

claim: Genotypes were called at 584,729 SNPs using apt-probeset-genotype.
source: We called genotypes at 584,729 SNPs using apt-probeset-genotype (Affymetrix) and standard settings.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the genotyping results.

claim: 53,148 VINOs were removed from the dataset.
source: We used the MouseDivGeno algorithm to identify variable intensity oligonucleotides (VINOs) (Yang et al., 2011); 53,148 VINOs were removed from the dataset.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data filtering results.

claim: After filtering steps, 156,204 SNPs were retained for mapping.
source: These filtering steps yielded 156,204 SNPs.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the final SNP dataset size.

claim: Ancestry inference used genotypes from 21 pure M. m. domesticus individuals and 22 M. m. musculus individuals.
source: To identify ancestry-informative SNPs, we compared genotypes from 21 pure M. m. domesticus individuals (11 from Massif Central, France and 10 from Cologne/Bonn, Germany) and 22 M. m. musculus individuals (11 from Námest nad Oslavou, Czech Republic and 11 from Almaty, Kazakhstan) (Staubach et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the reference populations used.

claim: Association mapping was performed using GEMMA, which fits a univariate mixed model incorporating an n x n relatedness matrix as a random effect.
source: We performed association mapping using GEMMA (Zhou and Stephens, 2012), which fits a univariate mixed model, incorporating an n x n relatedness (identity-by-state) matrix as a random effect to correct for genetic structure in the mapping population.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the statistical method used.

claim: Neither RTW nor expression PC1 was significantly correlated with age at phenotyping.
source: Neither RTW nor expression PC1 was significantly correlated with age at phenotyping (RTW: cor = −0.02, p = 0.72; PC1: cor = 0.01, p = 0.90), thus we did not include age in the model.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the relationship between phenotypes and age.

claim: Thresholds set to the fifth percentile across permutations for RTW were 5.73 × 10−7 (autosomes) and 5.83 × 10−5 (X chromosome).
source: Thresholds set to the fifth percentile across permutations for RTW were 5.73 × 10−7 (autosomes) and 5.83 × 10−5 (X chromosome); thresholds for expression PC1 were 1.66 × 10−8 (autosomes) and 1.01 × 10−5 (X chromosome).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the significance thresholds determined by permutation.

claim: Thresholds for expression PC1 were 1.66 × 10−8 (autosomes) and 1.01 × 10−5 (X chromosome).
source: Thresholds set to the fifth percentile across permutations for RTW were 5.73 × 10−7 (autosomes) and 5.83 × 10−5 (X chromosome); thresholds for expression PC1 were 1.66 × 10−8 (autosomes) and 1.01 × 10−5 (X chromosome).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the significance thresholds determined by permutation.

claim: The 10% false discovery rate threshold was equivalent to p = 3.49 × 10−5 for RTW and p = 2.86 × 10−4 for expression PC1.
source: Next, we identified regions using a more permissive significance threshold based on the 10% false discovery rate (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995), equivalent to p = 3.49 × 10−5 for RTW and p = 2.86 × 10−4 for expression PC1.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the FDR-based significance thresholds.

claim: Significant regions <10 Mb apart were combined into a single region.
source: We combined significant regions <10 Mb apart into a single region.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the region definition procedure.

claim: 692 pairs of SNPs were tested for interactions for relative testis weight.
source: We tested all pairs of significant SNPs located on different chromosomes for each phenotype (692 pairs RTW, 82,428 pairs expression PC1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number of interaction tests performed.

claim: 82,428 pairs of SNPs were tested for interactions for expression PC1.
source: We tested all pairs of significant SNPs located on different chromosomes for each phenotype (692 pairs RTW, 82,428 pairs expression PC1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number of interaction tests performed.

claim: Interactions were reported as significant for SNP pairs with p < 0.05 and FDR < 0.1 for interaction terms.
source: We report interactions as significant for SNP pairs with p < 0.05 and FDR < 0.1 for interaction terms (RTW: FDR < 0.1 ∼ p < 0.02; expression PC1: FDR < 0.09 ∼ p < 0.05).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the significance criteria for interactions.

claim: 100 autosomal–autosomal SNP pairs and 100 X–autosomal pairs were tested in simulations.
source: We tested 100 autosomal–autosomal SNP pairs (SNPs on different chromosomes) and 100 X–autosomal pairs (50 with domesticus X-linked sterile alleles and 50 with musculus X-linked sterile alleles).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the simulation design.

claim: The magnitude of the most severe phenotype in simulations (−2.3 standard deviations) is based on observed relative testis weights in the most severely affected males.
source: The magnitude of the most severe phenotype (−2.3 standard deviations) is based on observed relative testis weights in the most severely affected males.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the simulation parameters.

claim: 90,000 simulations were performed in total.
source: In total, 90,000 simulations were performed, (9 architectures × 100 SNP pairs × 100 data sets).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number of simulations.

claim: Using permutation-based significance thresholds, the median false positive rate was 0.014.
source: Using permutation-based significance thresholds, the median false positive rate was 0.014 (calculated for simulations with ≥10 SNPs within 50 Mb of either causative locus).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of simulation results.

claim: The median false positive rate was 0.280 using the FDR < 0.1 threshold.
source: By contrast, the median false positive rate was 0.280 using the FDR < 0.1 threshold, indicating this threshold is more permissive than predicted.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of simulation results.

claim: This is the first GWAS for a reproductive barrier trait.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first GWAS for a reproductive barrier trait.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study approach.

claim: This study provides the first genome-scale description of a hybrid incompatibility network in nature.
source: Moreover, this study provides the first genome-scale description of a hybrid incompatibility network in nature.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and scope of the study results.

claim: A total of 18,992/36,323 probes showed significant associations with at least one SNP.
source: A total of 18,992/36,323 probes showed significant associations with at least one SNP.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the eQTL mapping results.

claim: Trans eQTL are associated with sterility while cis eQTL are predominantly associated with subspecies differences.
source: We focused on trans associations (SNP is located on different chromosome from transcript), based on evidence from a study in F2 hybrids that trans expression QTL (eQTL) are associated with sterility while cis eQTL are predominantly associated with subspecies differences (Turner et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The threshold for SNPs significantly enriched for trans associations was set at the 95% percentile of significant probe association counts across all SNPs.
source: To identify SNPs significantly enriched for trans associations with expression, we used a threshold set at the 95% percentile of significant probe association counts across all SNPs (i.e., SNPs that showed associations with at least 30 transcripts, Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the threshold determination method.

claim: The combined mapping results provide multiple lines of evidence for contributions of all 50 PC1 regions and 9/12 testis weight regions.
source: The combined mapping results provide multiple lines of evidence for contributions of all 50 PC1 regions and 9/12 testis weight regions.
evidence: This claim is based on integration of multiple mapping results.

claim: The three testis-weight regions (RTW04, RTW05, RTW08) not significantly associated with testis expression phenotypes are more likely to be spurious and are weaker candidates for future study.
source: The three testis-weight regions (RTW04, RTW05, RTW08) not significantly associated with testis expression phenotypes are more likely to be spurious and are weaker candidates for future study.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of supporting evidence from multiple phenotypes.

claim: The Dobzhansky-Muller model predicts that the effect of each hybrid defect gene depends on interaction with at least one partner locus.
source: The Dobzhansky-Muller model predicts that the effect of each hybrid defect gene depends on interaction with at least one partner locus.
evidence: This is a statement about theoretical predictions from the Dobzhansky-Muller model.

claim: Power to identify pairwise epistasis in GWAS for quantitative traits is limited even with very large sample sizes, due to multiple testing issues.
source: Power to identify pairwise epistasis in GWAS for quantitative traits is limited even with very large sample sizes, due to multiple testing issues (e.g. Marchini et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study discussing statistical power for epistasis detection.

claim: Incompatibility alleles are not subject to negative selection within species and may be at high frequency or fixed within species.
source: Despite substantial deleterious effects in hybrids, incompatibility alleles are not subject to negative selection within species and may be at high frequency or fixed within species.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the population genetics of incompatibility alleles.

claim: The prevalence of affected individuals in a hybrid zone for epistatic traits may be much higher than for deleterious traits in pure populations.
source: Hence, the prevalence of affected individuals in a hybrid zone for epistatic traits may be much higher than for deleterious traits in pure populations (e.g. disease in humans).
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of incompatibility allele frequencies for mapping power.

claim: Combining mapping of multiple sterility-related phenotypes substantially improved power to identify sterility loci.
source: Combining mapping of multiple sterility-related phenotypes substantially improved power to identify sterility loci.
evidence: This claim is based on the observation that most loci showed associations with multiple phenotypes.

claim: Spurious associations are unlikely to be shared across phenotypes.
source: Spurious associations are unlikely to be shared across phenotypes, thus evidence from multiple phenotypes provided confidence for contributions of nine genomic regions to testis weight (on the X and 5 autosomes) and 50 genomic regions to expression PC1 (on the X and 18 autosomes).
evidence: This is a logical inference about the interpretation of overlapping associations.

claim: 8/12 testis-weight regions contain 10 or fewer protein-coding genes.
source: For example, 8/12 testis-weight regions and 28/50 expression PC1 regions contain 10 or fewer protein-coding genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene annotation analysis of GWAS regions.

claim: 28/50 expression PC1 regions contain 10 or fewer protein-coding genes.
source: For example, 8/12 testis-weight regions and 28/50 expression PC1 regions contain 10 or fewer protein-coding genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene annotation analysis of GWAS regions.

claim: Candidate genes with known roles in reproduction were identified in four testis-weight regions.
source: We identified candidate genes with known roles in reproduction in four testis-weight regions and 17 expression PC1 regions (Tables 1–2).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene annotation analysis shown in Tables 1-2.

claim: Candidate genes with known roles in reproduction were identified in 17 expression PC1 regions.
source: We identified candidate genes with known roles in reproduction in four testis-weight regions and 17 expression PC1 regions (Tables 1–2).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene annotation analysis shown in Tables 1-2.

claim: For the majority of regions (8/12 relative testis weight, 33/50 expression PC1), there are no overlapping/nearby genes previously linked to fertility.
source: However, for the majority of regions (8/12 relative testis weight, 33/50 expression PC1), there are no overlapping/nearby genes previously linked to fertility.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene annotation analysis.

claim: There is concordance between some of the genetic interactions between loci identified in hybrid zone mice and interactions identified by mapping in F2 hybrids.
source: There is concordance between some of the genetic interactions between loci identified here and interactions identified by mapping sterility phenotypes and testis expression traits in an F2 cross between musculus and domesticus (White et al., 2011; Turner et al., 2014) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with previous studies as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: An interaction between chromosome 12 and the central X chromosome (RTW11, PC49) identified for testis weight and expression PC1 overlaps an interaction affecting testis expression in F2 hybrids.
source: For example, an interaction between chromosome 12 and the central X chromosome (RTW11, PC49) identified for testis weight and expression PC1 overlaps an interaction affecting testis expression in F2 hybrids (Turner et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with a previous F2 study.

claim: The 4.3 Mb interval of overlap among chromosome 12 loci encompasses 12 protein-coding genes.
source: The 4.3 Mb interval of overlap among chromosome 12 loci (RTW07, PC29, 32.38–41.43 Mb F2s) encompasses 12 protein-coding genes, including a gene with a knockout model showing low testis weight and sperm count (Arl4a) (Schurmann et al., 2002), and two genes with roles in regulating gene expression (Meox2, Etv1).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene annotation analysis of the overlapping region.

claim: Five testis-weight regions overlap candidate regions from the hybrid zone genomic clines analysis.
source: Five testis-weight regions and 18 expression-PC1 regions overlap candidate regions from the hybrid zone genomic clines analysis (Tables 1–2), however, the patterns of overlap were not statistically significant (p > 0.05, 10,000 permutations).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with genomic cline analysis results.

claim: 18 expression-PC1 regions overlap candidate regions from the hybrid zone genomic clines analysis.
source: Five testis-weight regions and 18 expression-PC1 regions overlap candidate regions from the hybrid zone genomic clines analysis (Tables 1–2), however, the patterns of overlap were not statistically significant (p > 0.05, 10,000 permutations).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with genomic cline analysis results.

claim: The patterns of overlap between GWAS regions and hybrid zone genomic cline candidate regions were not statistically significant (p > 0.05, 10,000 permutations).
source: Five testis-weight regions and 18 expression-PC1 regions overlap candidate regions from the hybrid zone genomic clines analysis (Tables 1–2), however, the patterns of overlap were not statistically significant (p > 0.05, 10,000 permutations).
evidence: This claim is supported by permutation testing.

claim: The musculus derived X chromosome has been implicated repeatedly in genetic studies of sterility in F1 and F2 hybrids.
source: The musculus derived X chromosome has been implicated repeatedly in genetic studies of sterility in F1 and F2 hybrids (Reviewed in Good et al. (2008a); White et al. (2011)).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles and studies.

claim: A testis expression-QTL mapping study performed in F2s showed that domesticus ancestry in the central/distal region of the X was associated with a sterile expression pattern.
source: A testis expression-QTL mapping study performed in F2s also showed that domesticus ancestry in the central/distal region of the X was associated with a sterile expression pattern (Turner et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous F2 study.

claim: Differences between studies might reflect geographic variation in sterility alleles, but identification of domesticus-sterile X alleles only in generations beyond the F1 suggests that interactions with recessive autosomal partner loci are essential.
source: Differences between studies might reflect geographic variation in sterility alleles, but identification of domesticus-sterile X alleles only in generations beyond the F1 suggests that interactions with recessive autosomal partner loci are essential.
evidence: This is an inference about the genetic architecture based on comparison of results across studies.

claim: The importance of recessive sterility alleles was demonstrated previously by the discovery of multiple novel recessive loci in an F2 mapping study.
source: The importance of recessive sterility alleles was demonstrated previously by the discovery of multiple novel recessive loci in an F2 mapping study (White et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Loci causing male sterility in Drosophila pseudoobscura Bogota–USA hybrids have multiple interaction partners; seven loci of varying effect size interact to cause sterility.
source: Loci causing male sterility in Drosophila pseudoobscura Bogota–USA hybrids also have multiple interaction partners; seven loci of varying effect size interact to cause sterility (Phadnis, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study in Drosophila.

claim: In hybrids between Drosophila koepferae and Drosophila buzzatii, sterility is associated with many loci of small effect, consistent with a polygenic threshold model.
source: In hybrids between Drosophila koepferae and Drosophila buzzatii, sterility is associated with many loci of small effect, consistent with a polygenic threshold model (Moran and Fontdevila, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study in Drosophila.

claim: Biological pathways/networks are often affected by multiple Dobzhansky–Muller interactions.
source: These studies suggest that biological pathways/networks are often affected by multiple Dobzhansky–Muller interactions; a single pairwise interaction between incompatible alleles disrupts pathway function enough to cause a hybrid defect phenotype, but when more incompatible alleles are present the effects of multiple pairwise interactions are synergistic.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of multiple interactions observed in this and other studies.

claim: Variation in the effect sizes of sterility loci might reflect variation in the number of networks in which the gene is involved and the connectedness/centrality of the gene within those networks.
source: Variation in the effect sizes of sterility loci might then reflect variation in the number of networks in which the gene is involved and the connectedness/centrality of the gene within those networks.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the relationship between network properties and effect sizes.

claim: A 'snowball effect'—faster-than-linear accumulation of incompatibilities caused by epistasis—is predicted on the basis of the Dobzhansky–Muller model.
source: A 'snowball effect'—faster-than-linear accumulation of incompatibilities caused by epistasis—is predicted on the basis of the Dobzhansky–Muller model (Orr, 1995; Orr and Turelli, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: Patterns of accumulation of hybrid incompatibilities in Drosophila and Solanum provide empirical support for the snowball hypothesis.
source: Patterns of accumulation of hybrid incompatibilities in Drosophila and Solanum provide empirical support for the snowball hypothesis (Matute et al., 2010; Moyle and Nakazato, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: The results are not consistent with the assumption of the snowball model that incompatibilities are independent.
source: Because most GWAS regions have many interaction partners, our results are not consistent with the assumption of the snowball model that incompatibilities are independent, suggesting that network models of incompatibilities (Johnson and Porter, 2000; Porter and Johnson, 2002; Johnson and Porter, 2007; Palmer and Feldman, 2009) may be more accurate for understanding the evolution of reproductive barriers in house mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed pattern of multiple interactions per locus.

claim: Network models of incompatibilities may be more accurate for understanding the evolution of reproductive barriers in house mice.
source: Because most GWAS regions have many interaction partners, our results are not consistent with the assumption of the snowball model that incompatibilities are independent, suggesting that network models of incompatibilities (Johnson and Porter, 2000; Porter and Johnson, 2002; Johnson and Porter, 2007; Palmer and Feldman, 2009) may be more accurate for understanding the evolution of reproductive barriers in house mice.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed interaction patterns and citations to network models.

claim: Because deleterious effects of a sterility allele are not dependent on a single partner allele, the marginal effect of each locus and thus visibility to selection are less sensitive to the allele frequencies at any single partner locus in the population.
source: Because deleterious effects of a sterility allele are not dependent on a single partner allele, the marginal effect of each locus and thus visibility to selection are less sensitive to the allele frequencies at any single partner locus in the population.
evidence: This is an inference about the evolutionary implications of multiple interactions per locus.

claim: General features of the genetic architecture of hybrid sterility—the number of incompatibilities and number and effect size of interacting loci—are arguably more likely to be shared among organisms than specific hybrid sterility genes.
source: General features of the genetic architecture of hybrid sterility—the number of incompatibilities and number and effect size of interacting loci—are arguably more likely to be shared among organisms than specific hybrid sterility genes.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about comparative patterns in speciation genetics.

claim: Comparison of genetic architecture features among taxa may reveal commonalities of the speciation process.
source: Comparison of these features among taxa may reveal commonalities of the speciation process.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the value of comparative studies.
